The effectiveness of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in producing visually realistic images has been confirmed across a variety of domains.  Despite this success, generating images with spatially consistent environmental details has been found to be extremely challenging. In this study, an alternative to the standard GAN approach is presented by integrating a Hidden Space with dynamic switching probabilities. The HS-GAN architecture includes an HS module that represents environmental features as dynamic switching probabilities, an ES module for estimating these probabilities, an ES network that produces the current HS state given the current probability, and an EG module for producing the generated image given the HS state. The HS-GAN model is capable of adapting to changes in environmental features while producing a realistic image. The study demonstrates the applicability of the HS-GAN model to learning and producing synthetic images with accurate spatially consistent environmental features. Utilizing a dataset of images with realistic natural scenery and conditions, the model is tested for its ability to produce a realistic image with accurate environmental features under various condition changes. The generated images and their corresponding true images are visually compared to assess realism. The study also examines the effects of the HS-GAN model configuration on its performance by analyzing the role of the HS and ES modules through a sensitivity analysis. The HS-GAN model is found to be a reliable approach for producing a realistic image with dynamic environmental features. The implementation details of the model can significantly affect its performance. The most effective module configuration of the HS-GAN model was found to be the EG module with an M1 configuration, producing a higher PNS score by 9.4% compared to the baseline. The study demonstrates the applicability of the HS-GAN model to the problem of generating images with accurate spatially consistent environmental details. The generated images produced by the HS-GAN model are of high realism with a PNS score comparable to the true images. The study opens up possibilities for the integration of the HS-GAN model in a variety of image-based applications such as synthetic image generation in computer vision and image processing. The integration of the HS-GAN model to the synthetic image generation process can significantly improve the accuracy and level of detail of the generated images. The study presents a new perspective on the problem of generating images with accurate spatially consistent environmental features and the implementation details of the HS-GAN model. The understanding of the problem of generating images with accurate spatially consistent environmental features and the effects of the HS-GAN model configuration on its performance can significantly improve the accuracy and level of detail of the generated images. A widely employed technique in computing Bayesian credible intervals is Nested Sampling. Nested Sampling works by eliminating samples with lower likelihood, leaving a posterior distribution in a region that approximates the volume of the posterior distribution in the given range of likelihood levels. The method is highly dependent on the step selector, which determines the samples to be excluded. We investigate the performance of various step selectors and introduce two new methods: the "Likelihood-Leap" and "Probability-Push" algorithms. We evaluate these selectors against established methods, including the "Sort-by-Likelihood" and a random selection approach, within different scenarios. Our research examines the response of each selector to diverse scenarios, focusing on the section of the distribution, likelihood levels, posterior geometry, and residual samples. We found the "Sort-by-Likelihood" selector to be generally more effective than the others, although the "Likelihood-Leap" and "Probability-Push" methods demonstrate reliability in specific scenarios. We also found that the "Sort-by-Likelihood" selector outperforms others when the distribution is sectioned below the likelihood level and when the residual samples include the mode, but it struggles when the distribution is sectioned above the likelihood level and when the residual samples exclude the mode. In these scenarios, the "Probability-Push" selector becomes more reliable. Conversely, the "Likelihood-Leap" selector becomes more reliable when the distribution is sectioned above the likelihood level and when the residual samples exclude the mode. These new selectors can enhance Nested Sampling performance, but their effectiveness depends on the specific scenario. Moreover, the results of this research can be utilized to refine random selection, leading to more reliable results in diverse scenarios. Random selection that prioritizes lower likelihoods in demographic sectioning and residual samples that include the mode tends to be more reliable. Conversely, the random selection that prioritizes higher likelihoods in demographic sectioning and residual samples that exclude the mode tends to be less reliable. In addition, the results of this research can be applied to other methods that eliminate samples with lower likelihoods. We suggest that the lower likelihoods that contribute the least to the posterior distribution in the given range of likelihood levels. Furthermore, the results of this research can be applied to other methods that eliminate samples based on different criteria, such as the Maximum a-Posteriori method. We found that the "Sort-by-Likelihood" selector tends to outperform others in sectioning below the likelihood level, and this knowledge can be utilized to refine Maximum a-Posteriori search. In fault-tolerant distance labeling, an algorithm labels vertices of a graph that can withstand vertex failures, providing accurate distance information even after one vertex fails. For planar graphs with an arbitrary number of labels, we developed a fault-resilient distance labeling system that requires at most a polylogarithmic number of labels. This labels can be applied quickly in a worst-case time of $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ for $n$ vertices, an improvement over previous work. Even though we cannot achieve a much better time of $\widetilde{O}(n)$ with our current method, the distance labels we developed allow for efficient updating after failures in constant time. Furthermore, we cannot find a better fault-resilient system using standard graph models as we can apply our system to graphs without a minimum degree or a fixed architecture. Using advanced graph structures, we developed an even more efficient labeling system that requires at least $\Omega(n)$ labels. This labeling system can be applied in quasi-linear time but requires a more complex graph structure. Lastly, we developed a fault-resilient search algorithm in graphs that can withstand any $\epsilon n$ failures, an improvement over previous work. This algorithm can be applied in time that is almost linear, an improvement over previous work. An earlier version of this work was presented at FUN 2014. This work was supported by research funds from an NSFC Grant and an NNSF Grant. A video illustrating the algorithmic concept can be found at https://youtu.be/1kHgU0p6s9g under the title "FUN2014-Labeling-Graphs-under-Vertex-Deletions". In this study, the two-particle correlations of the Bose-Hubbard model under both deterministic and random noise forces are examined in detail. Particular emphasis is placed on the time-dependent pair distribution function $g_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{x},t)$. It is found that even in the presence of dissipation, this function can exhibit revivals reminiscent of their closed system counterparts. Furthermore, spatial analysis of $g_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{x},t)$ reveals that noise can cause fluctuations in the pair wave packet's spatial profile as it evolves over time. By exploring time-domain correlations, it is discovered that one-dimensional lattices displaying $g_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{x},t) < 3$ can revitalize. Additionally, an optimal superfluid regime in the context of noise-strength, lattice size, and non-integer frequency ratios in two-dimensional lattices is identified. These results are consistent when observed in both the time-domain and frequency-domain, showcasing the potential for distinguishing between coherent and incoherent processes using the Eberly-Lewenstein quantum memoryless laser model. Lastly, an investigation into the effects of non-Markovian dynamics, model assumptions, and realistic lattice potential limitations is performed. These results may contribute to the development of novel quantum-based technologies and serve as a foundation for exploring quantum dynamics in the context of realistic, driven quantum systems. The relevant data and code are available via GitHub at https://github.com/steve-russell/EBFL-model-driven. The corresponding video is available at https://youtu.be/8H7pYV7_3Gk. We provide specific conditions under which a weak solution exists for a given elliptic equation in divergence form that involves an $L^2$ measure and an obstacle with elliptic regime. Furthermore, we establish the connection between the set of weak solutions and the dual problem of a related obstacle inequality, using tools such as currents and tangential surfaces. Additionally, we prove that the set of weak solutions is compact in a suitable topology. These results are then applied to a measure-trace problem, and the existing results from [11] are improved and extended to the related linear problem. Finally, the findings are also utilized to address a nonlinear problem that involves a Boltzmann equation in divergence form with $L^2$ measure and an obstacle with elliptic regime. The nonlinear problem is related to a dual problem that describes a quantity that flows along an obstacle, subject to elliptical regime conditions. By applying the existing theory of varifolds, we achieve the desired results for the nonlinear problem. Ultimately, the compactness of the set of weak solutions for the nonlinear problem is established in a suitable topology. The work presented enhances the existing theory of elliptic equations in divergence form, particularly with regard to measure-trace and flow-around-obstacles scenarios. It is notable that the results presented generalize and extend various recent findings in the literature on nonlinear elliptic equations, identifying key conditions for their validity. Moreover, the existing theory of dual problems for elliptic equations in divergence form is deepened and expanded through the introduction of a unique current measure with significant implications for its regularity, well-posedness, and relation to varifold currents. The work presaged the recent advancements in elliptic equations with measure-trace in divergence form that have been achieved through the research of C. Calderon and M. Ciakeki. By establishing the findings presented above, the compactness of the set of weak solutions for elliptic equations in the specified contexts is demonstrated in a suitable topology. The existing theory of elliptic equations in divergence form is thus enhanced and generalized. To identify out-of-distribution (OoD) samples effectively, it is crucial to recognize that OoD samples may be slightly different from in-distribution samples, rather than being drastically distinct. Consequently, instead of strictly separating OoD samples from training data, we aim to categorize them within controllable "layers" or strata of reduced complexity. By revisiting the regression function's variation within these strata, we refine the Mean Squared Error (MSE) upper bound that leverages data coverage and kernel properties, similar to previous work. Notably, this bound improves upon existing ones by eliminating unnecessary restrictions, revealing the underlying structure of these strata as a semi-definite program with a Gaussian process (GP) kernel as its kernel. Building upon this insight, we develop new detection methods by training multiple GPs using labeled samples from each strata, along with unsupervised techniques that estimate the GP kernels' parameters across strata and even unlabelled in-distribution data. Experimental findings confirm that these methods outperform existing approaches, reconcile anomalies in known bounds, and withstand a range of synthetic and real-world challenges in robustness and generalization. The proposed method's implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andreaspberger/dgnet. Furthermore, detailed numerical findings and additional results can be found at https://distr-gp-strata.github.io. As the proposed research consolidates several lines of work, it is expected to contribute significantly to the field. Notably, the expected improvement in detection accuracy can be quantified for specific datasets, and the method's performance is expected to be comparable to state-of-the-art approaches for datasets such as CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100, PACS, and LSUN-R. The research is anticipated to spark future developments in GP-based strata and out-of-distribution detection, ultimately advancing the field towards more precise upper bounds and state-of-the-art detection methods. The general audience is assumed to have a foundational understanding of mathematical and computational concepts. The research is presented in a clear, entry-level manner, with a narrative structure that begins with an overview of the field, only to reveal that existing work has inherent limitations. Consequently, the method relies on refined versions of a novel GP-based regression function's variation analysis, offering a significant contribution to the field. The research culminates with numerical findings and a public implementation, positioning the method as a promising foundation for future work. Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how these functions manipulate the positioning of feature pairs. Breaking down pair-wise gradient updates this way enables a deeper understanding of the dominant effects and commonalities across different loss functions. Building on this insight, we've developed an approach to merge and create new loss functions by combining their individual characteristics. Experimental evaluations using the CUB-200 birds dataset verify the accuracy in analyzing and combining these loss functions. Moreover, our method has yielded four combined loss functions which, when used, significantly boost the top-1 accuracy of CUB-200 from 76.1% to 80.3%. In our research, we develop a new method to create approximations of holographic error correction codes using a specific type of tensor network architecture, hyper-invariant MERA. This approach allows us to tightly constraint the computational efficiency of these complex codes, using a specific power-law dependency for certain error thresholds. Utilizing a quantum query model, we establish a lower limit on the computational complexity required to achieve these thresholds. Our findings apply to a broad range of holographic error correction code families, including holographic Gaussian codes and stacked codes, providing insights into the fundamental limitations of these complex codes. Furthermore, we explore the interplay between system size, query complexity, and error thresholds, as well as investigate how approximations of these codes can be achieved by adjusting the density of tensor product states within the tensor network. This density can be modified using a simple algorithm based on a basic quantum query operation. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through simulations of a holographic Gaussian code family, supporting our theoretical findings. Last but not least, we discuss the implications of our research on the theoretical lower limits of error correction efficiency, as well as its potential applications in near-term quantum computing and simulations. This research opens up new avenues for investigating the efficiency of quantum information processing tasks, especially for currently unknown error correction code families. Additionally, we suggest future research directions at the end of the paper.

This results in a time lag between when the environment sends a signal and when the receiver processes it. We overcome the challenge posed by these delays by developing a strategy that exploits the relationship between signal processing times and the effectiveness of the signals. This setting, characterized by decisions made at the earlier signal arrival times by the environment, is referred to as the delayed setting. We focus on finding non-stochastic (optimal) policies for both the advisor and the environment in this context. We first prove that every instance of this problem has a solution. We also investigate two specific scenarios with special relationships between signal processing times and signals. We develop a strategy for these cases, as well as a general combinatorial algorithm for when signal processing times are non-decreasing. We show the effectiveness of our algorithms by proving they are optimal in these scenarios and provide bounds on their performance. We also prove that our algorithm's performance is nearly optimal in all cases. We believe our method will be a valuable starting point for future studies on delayed settings with more complex relationships between signal processing times and signals. We also investigate how well the CLUAD and DELAYED algorithms perform in these cases and find that their performance is closely related to the processing delays. Naturalistic driving studies have traditionally relied on various evaluation methods, but a critical component - the driving situation - has often been overlooked. This data deficit has hindered researchers in understanding the characteristics of dangerous driving situations. To address this gap, our study presents the Situation-based Naturalistic Driving Dataset (SceNDD), a groundbreaking dataset designed to capture essential aspects of driving scenarios. This comprehensive dataset comprises four distinctive fields: comprehensive situation information, vehicle observations, sensor readings, and video footage. By utilizing cutting-edge technology, SceNDD was collected from a fleet of 25 vehicles equipped with state-of-the-art safety systems, which drove through Dutch roads for three years. This resulting dataset spans 13 terabytes of content in three distinct components, allowing us to develop a sophisticated data extraction pipeline and create a comprehensive dataset describing 1.7 million driving scenarios. This dataset serves as a valuable resource for various applications, empowering models to anticipate and respond to driving-related events. To further understand the structure of driving scenarios, we employed an unsupervised clustering method and discovered distinct groups representing specific situation types. This analysis highlights promising directions for future data-driven research and sheds light on the essential characteristics of driving scenarios. Building upon SceNDD and the insights gained from our analysis, we propose a data-driven approach to predict the likelihood of certain safety events. This predicted safety event is then incorporated into the situation description. Additionally, to facilitate easy data access, we have developed a user-friendly data browser to accompany the SceNDD dataset. This browser enables researchers to visually explore the dataset, gain insights into the characteristics of individual situation categories, and gain inspiration for future data-driven applications. The presented dataset, data extraction pipeline, and data analysis provide a foundation for future data-driven research to fill the gap between driving data and situation information. The SceNDD dataset and associated data access browser can be downloaded from: https://github.com/keoofy/SceNDD/tree/master/SceNDD. This study has been completed in conjunction with Shoendel, a Dutch organization focused on promoting Shareable Data in the transportation sector, with the goal of fostering a data-sharing community. Specifically, our study aims to contribute the SceNDD dataset to the growing collection of naturalistic driving studies, advancing the understanding of driving scenarios. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with the rapid proliferation of the virus being exacerbated by human mobility. To combat this, many governments have adopted contact tracing methods, with the utilization of mobile technology serving as a key strategy for tracking COVID-19's spread. Contact tracing mobile apps, such as those using Bluetooth technology, were developed to aid the public health response efforts; however, these apps' reliance on location data poses significant risks to users' privacy. This could lead to societal stigma, stalking, and the potential for government misuse, with prominent instances of privacy breach occurring in countries like South Korea and India. Despite the existing literature on contact tracing COVID-19 apps, a prominent case involving Brazil, where a national contact tracing COVID-19 app called "Coronavirus-SUS", is presented as an example to illustrate how easy it is to track users' locations, connecting Bluetooth devices can compromise a person's life, leading to a potential loss of means. This analysis is performed by a cybersecurity group, which identified vulnerabilities similar to those of the widely discussed contact tracing COVID-19 app "DeeSaúde", while discussing the differences between national and international contact tracing COVID-19 apps and highlighting how these vulnerabilities pose a significant risk to users' privacy. Moreover, a potential misuse of location data was demonstrated by the team, with suggestions provided to the developers on how to enhance the "Coronavirus-SUS" app's privacy protection mechanisms. This study serves as an opportunity to analyze a national contact tracing COVID-19 app's security and privacy features through a reverse engineering approach, with a goal to evaluate whether the "Coronavirus-SUS" app's developers had implemented adequate measures to safeguard users' location data and the app itself. This research aims to investigate how effectively COVID-19 contact tracing apps are in preserving users' anonymity, with a focus on the "Coronavirus-SUS" app's and its potential for proper functioning; the study also delves into the legal and ethical standards that COVID-19 contact tracing apps must adhere to in Brazil. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute valuable findings that can inspire future work and promote a more detailed analysis and evaluation of contact tracing COVID-19 apps' security and privacy features. A study on the (39991) Iochroma asteroid family's origin is presented. Research indicates that this asteroid family is linked to a specific resonance with the 3:1 mean motion, specifically 3:1-(L+G), where L represents the longitude of the Laplace space, and G represents the longitude of the heating source. Notably, the source of heating, Iochroma, is a unique asteroid characterized by a unique arrangement, featuring two interconnected equal masses, positioned at the ends of a rigid rod, and a third unconnected mass, situated at the end of the rod. This unique configuration causes unusual thermal interactions.  In addition, the study found another member of the Iochroma family, (39992) Ioviana, associated with the 5:3-(L+G) mean motion resonance. The origin of the Ioviana family is attributed to a 5:3 resonance triggered by a collision. The outcome of the collision results in a significant irreversibility that prevents the Ioviana family from experiencing precession reversal. The predicted time of the Ioviana family formation is estimated to be around 3.6 billion years ago. Furthermore, the Ioviana family shares a common evolutionary path with another asteroid family called Coronia, formed through a 1:5-(L+G) mean motion resonance. The formation of the Ioviana-Coronia subfamily of the Ioviana-Iochroma sequence marks the beginning of the Ioviana-Iochroma shared evolution. The formation time of the Ioviana-Iochroma sequence is estimated to be around 3.8 billion years ago. The Ioviana-Iochroma shared evolution, resulting from a collision that triggered a 5:3 mean motion resonance, might be responsible for the unique thermal characteristics observed in Ioviana and other members of the Ioviana-Iochroma sequence. Interestingly, the Ioviana-Iochroma sequence of asteroids shares a common origin with another collision that formed the Coronia family, resulting in the Ioviana-Coronia asteroid family. The predicted time of the Ioviana-Coronia formation is estimated to be around 3.8 billion years ago. Prior to the Ioviana-Coronia formation, the Ioviana-Iochroma sequence of asteroids had already existed for around 200 million years. Analysis of the light curves confirms that all members of the Ioviana-Iochroma sequence of asteroids are of non-primitive non-chondritic composition.

We establish conditions under which a linear group defined over a number field has the charm property, ensuring that any solvable subgroup maintains a fixed factor over a restricted, finite set of fields. Our proof relies on an invariance property of solvable subgroups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that inner forms of semisimple groups are charmable, as well as several special cases, including general linear and symplectic groups. A crucial concept introduced herein is stiffness, which we define for a group $G$. If a solvable subgroup of $G$ has the stiffness property, then it will maintain a fixed factor over a particular set of fields. We show that all subgroups of a stiff group are stiff as well. Using proof-by-contradiction, we construct examples of stiff subgroups of solvable groups. Our work generalizes and enhances existing results by Borel, Serre, and others. Additionally, we build upon Tamagawa's theorem, reinterpreting it as a charmable transfer of invariants from the adelic to the arithmetic realm. Our findings imply new cases of the Tits indecomposability theorem and the Kneser conjecture. We also achieve the following complementary results: the uniqueness of certain maximal subgroups; the existence of group extensions with specified properties; cases of the Richardson elementarity; the existence of decompositions of character fields; and the injectivity of the Galois group action on certain fields. Finally, our work yields novel functional equations for the lengths of representations and the sizes of orbits. Additionally, we prove an analogue of the Zariski-Lul theorem for general linear groups and show that certain arithmetic groups possess a compact model. The latter result generalizes a finding by Platonov and Fawaz. Our theoretical findings are accompanied by practical computations, exemplified by a determination of the 2-part of the Brauer group of the function field of the modular j-line. The success of a movie is determined by various factors, some of which are difficult to influence even with substantial resources. Understanding which attributes are most significant for predicting a movie's revenue can aid in making more informed decisions during the pre-release phase. A larger dataset of 2037 movies was used to investigate the impact of specific predictable features on domestic box office revenue. Our results indicate that movies with established acting talent, directed by experienced filmmakers, and belonging to established genres tend to earn higher domestic revenues. Notably, our research also reveals that having a well-known cast appears to have a negative correlation with revenue, likely due to the inherent competition among the involved actors. These findings were utilized to develop a predictive model for movie success, enabling the identification of movies with the greatest potential for achieving high domestic box office grosses during the pre-release phase. Specifically, our analysis identified attributes that distinguished successful and unsuccessful movies, and our quantitative results revealed that certain cinematic elements (such as genre and visual effects) and qualitative attributes (such as ratings from notable critics) significantly influenced movie revenue. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that an additional feature, already available before the release, can augment the accuracy of our quantitative attributes-based model for predicting movie success. Interestingly, our analysis also highlights that having a lower budget does not necessarily impede a movie's ability to achieve high domestic box office grosses, as exemplified by successful low-budget films such as the dark fantasy movie "Hellboy" and the science fiction film "John Wick". These findings were further validated by comparing our results with actual box office data. A systematic replication study was conducted by employing a distinct dataset to ensure the generalizability of our conclusions. By employing Bayesian statistics to test for evidence, our research confirmed that some of the distinguished attributes were actually correlated with movie success, providing a transparent explanation for the findings that contradicted our initial results. Ultimately, our application of systematic research methods to a large dataset enabled us to derive evidence-based conclusions about the attributes influencing movie success, thus expanding our understanding of this domain. Importantly, our research revealed that some of the distinguished attributes were actually related to each other, suggesting the presence of underlying processes. Consequently, our application of the techniques employed in machine learning, such as decision tree analysis, was motivated by a desire to uncover the causal mechanisms driving the results. The design acknowledges that a linear model is insufficient to capture non-linear patterns in time series data, which is why it integrates a sparse, regularized coefficient matrix with a time-varying factor model. The proposed matrix's diagonal entries alone endow it with the ability to respond to acute shifts in the time series. Through a generated mixture of Gaussians prior, the model infuses hidden state representations with sparsity. Densely structured factors enable daily/continual hidden states, while sparsely structured ones detect acutely changing variables at specific times, providing more information than existing sparse models. The model employs a hybrid RNN-BN back-end to forecast future observations based on the extracted key time points. The proposed model's performance is evaluated against state-of-the-art models on two datasets, yielding notably better forecasting results. The research also includes an analysis of the sparse structure of the estimated coefficient matrix and how it correlates with real-time data changes. The findings indicate that the proposed model achieves a satisfactory trade-off between interpretability and performance, due in part to the sparse structure of the time series data, which facilitates understanding of the forecasting results. Object detection capabilities have advanced significantly with the development of next-generation techniques. Current detection methods rely on large, category-specific training datasets and often struggle with unidentified object categories. This study proposes a new paradigm for open-vocabulary object detection using pseudo-training labels in the form of bounding boxes. We've found that fine-tuning a pre-trained model with pseudo labels is an effective approach, but the quality of the labels matters. By employing an unsupervised object-level feature extractor, we can improve the accuracy of pseudo labels and facilitate better training. Our proposed method has been successfully tested on the CUB-200-2011 and Characteraug dataset, producing superior results compared to baseline methods. The research code will be publicly available on the GitHub platform.

Human-assisted translation is an essential component of machine translation post-processing. To improve the efficiency of human-assisted translation, the reliability of translators is a significant consideration. Prior studies focused mainly on measuring translator reliability for the entire translation task, but did not explore how to apply machine learning models to assess reliability on a per-sample basis. Our research establishes a Bayesian method for evaluating translator reliability on a sample-by-sample basis. Moreover, we create a collection of parallel human and machine translations, and utilize this data within a Bayesian framework to determine the translator's level of proficiency. Our model enables the calculation of a translator's probability of accurately translating a given sentence. Additionally, our method allows for sampling an infinite number of translations, even for less experienced translators, to provide a more realistic estimation. Furthermore, our method can handle a translator's proficiency function being non-linear. By employing our established method, we analyze the translator's proficiency for both professional and non-professional translators. Our method also outperforms existing methods in estimating the test-set accuracy of both translators. For further details on our method and experimental results, please refer to our study. We establish a comprehensive formula linking the total energy absorbed with random matrix theory in systems that scatter energy, for both time-dependent and -independent inputs. This formula reveals that the likelihood of significant energy being focused at a specific point is inversely related to the total energy absorbed, to the power of -1/2. This result, which extends previous work on channel correlations in scattering systems, also enables the creation of algorithms to identify and analyze the most efficient pathways, referred to as eigenchannels. Utilizing random matrix theory, we develop two distinct methods, labelled method 1 and method 2, both of which are capable of accurately reconstructing eigenchannels even when the total energy absorbed is close to its maximum possible value. Notably, both techniques can be applied to systems that operate in an energy-independent manner, without requiring any initial optimization. Furthermore, we derive a mathematical proof illustrating that the sum of the most efficient pathways, as calculated using both method 1 and method 2, is directly proportional to the total energy absorbed. As a consequence, a significant percentage of the total energy absorbed can be localized at a specific point, without requiring any optimization. We verified these findings both theoretically and experimentally, in systems that operate in an energy-independent manner, without the use of any optimization procedures. Radio link failure data, which is typically based on binary failure/non-failure labels, can be notoriously difficult to work with when trying to predict wireless capacity and throughput. One potential solution is to treat these labels as continuous measurements of signal strength. We investigate the use of a specific type of machine learning network, called a deep convolutional neural network, for making this type of radio link prediction. By drawing a parallel with standard propagation models, we explore the use of a two-dimensional spatial architecture, which takes into account the distance between transceivers, and also a one-dimensional approach, which uses a simplified distance metric. In our analysis, we primarily focus on the key factor of tower height. Our results, which demonstrate notable performance gains over existing models, also suggest that additional spatial features could further improve predictions. We hope that our approach will serve as a starting point for developing more sophisticated networks, ultimately leading to a better understanding of signal strength and interference. We publicly release the relevant Python code on the online platform GitHub.

The process involves refining an initial, potentially insufficient search query into a more informed one, by utilizing more than one keyword. A new system called STRICT is introduced, combining a well-established IR tool with a designed ranking system to achieve concept location. The IR component transforms raw search data into relevant and focused search keywords. Subsequently, the ranking system selects the most suitable set of these keywords to produce an optimized search query. A prototype of STRICT was developed and tested on a small software project, demonstrating its ability to achieve concept location. Furthermore, a study comparing STRICT with a baseline IR approach was conducted, highlighting the STRICT's superiority based on search query quality and IR score, and supporting its effectiveness across different levels of search data and relevant information. Notably, the results showed that STRICT was beneficial even with limited relevant information in the dataset. A subsequent cost-benefit analysis was also performed, indicating that the additional search cost incurred by STRICT was justified due to its ability to achieve concept location. Based on the findings, it is suggested that STRICT be used as a secondary search aid to refine initially insufficient search queries. Notably, the proposed system represents the first integration of IR-based keyword identification for concept location. A comprehensive understanding of concept location and IR search were developed, and several search strategies were explored before proposing a novel combination of IR tool with ranking system. When subjected to ultrasonic vibrations, both static and oscillatory stresses can be applied and measured. To guarantee a match, researchers often create numerous, albeit unimportant, suggestions in the stable marriage problem. This scenario can occur when individuals have relatively limited choices, and researchers are interested in prioritizing high-quality matches over insignificant ones. A straightforward modification to the deferred acceptance algorithm achieves this priority, by giving more serious options priority over less serious ones as the algorithm progresses. By introducing a function that measures the relative importance of each individual, this modified algorithm guarantees a stable match while improving the overall match quality for all participants. Under specific conditions, this modified algorithm also achieves optimal results. Furthermore, this approach is applicable to a range of scenarios, including the famous "plenty of men, scarce skills" scenario, where it yields a substantial improvement in match quality, often by as much as 30% in complex instances. In addition, our technique is not only limited to the stable marriage problem but can also be applied to a broader range of matching scenarios. A simplified version of our approach, called "early rejection," is also computationally efficient and easy to implement. A comprehensive comparison of our approach and other existing techniques has been conducted, and the results have been verified using a vast range of real-world data sets that are now publicly available for further study. Current assessment methods for abstraction and summarization are inadequate, prompting the need for a more comprehensive and diverse evaluation of summaries. To address this, we introduce SummScore, a high-discriminative-z score (HDZ) based evaluation metric, designed to predict human ratings for human-generated and machine-generated summaries. Unlike other metrics, SummScore surpasses human judgment alignment without relying on reference summaries, instead employing a pre-trained Cross-Encoder to compare summaries with their corresponding source materials. Through an experiment involving multiple evaluation metrics and human ratings on four datasets, we validate the effectiveness of SummScore, observing that its correlation with human judgment reaches 0.846, demonstrating improved performance compared to other metrics. Furthermore, SummScore showcases enhanced robustness and versatility across various evaluation scenarios, encompassing diverse summary types and domains. Building upon SummScore, we develop it into an open-source tool, available for download at https://github.com/atenNascent/SummScore. We then, based on SummScore's evaluation results, establish a public leaderboard for abstractive summarization systems at https://github.com/atenNascent/SummScore. To date, leading systems have failed to achieve optimal performance according to SummScore's evaluation. We believe that our work contributes significantly to the development of a versatile and high-precision assessment method, aiming to stimulate future research in this area. Current 3D object detection models often employ LiDAR data alone due to reliability and cost considerations, despite sensor fusion offering potential performance gains. The interaction between an ultrashort laser pulse and a transparent liquid gives rise to a complex thermal gradient. Because the absorption of energy occurs over a broader area than the laser beam itself, the resulting self-induced diffraction pattern is shaped by the specific characteristics of this thermal gradient. When the laser pulse is applied to the liquid's surface, it creates a central region with normal thermal distribution in the direction of propagation, but one that exhibits a nonlinear temperature profile in the perpendicular direction due to the phenomenon of laser-induced breakdown. As the laser pulse travels deeper into the liquid, this nonlinear region expands, resulting in the observation of a broadening self-induced diffraction pattern in parallel laser experiments and the observation of complex, alternating maxima and minima in perpendicular experiments. According to our analysis, the intensity of these maxima decreases in accordance with the four-halves power law, while the distance between them and the point of laser incidence grows in accordance with a linear relationship. Furthermore, the width of the main diffraction maximum in parallel experiments has been discovered to be directly linked to the energy of the laser pulse. Our investigation provides the initial comprehensive analysis of the laser-induced thermal profile in a liquid and the self-induced diffraction effect. As a result, the findings of our research can serve as the foundation for a more in-depth understanding of the laser-induced thermal profile in a liquid and the self-induced diffraction effect. Moreover, the results can facilitate the development of novel methods for measuring particle size. Specifically, when the thermal gradient is shaped into a slab, the intensity of the main minimum in parallel experiments has been discovered to be directly linked to the energy of the laser pulse, while the distance between this minimum and the point of laser incidence grows in accordance with a linear relationship. Furthermore, the width of the main minimum in parallel experiments has been discovered to be inversely linked to the energy of the laser pulse. Further investigations have demonstrated the feasibility of generating alternating phase states within a liquid, which has allowed for the observation and analysis (using a well-known model) of fundamental signs of spontaneous symmetry breaking. Shaping the laser pulse in a cylindrical form has led to the observation of a wider range of diffraction patterns than in parallel experiments. Deep neural networks have shown impressive performance in control-related tasks, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by the lack of conventional validation methods. This paper examines the applicability of control community-driven validation methods, such as open-loop and input-guided testing, in assessing neural networks. It is often challenging to achieve a high success rate with these methods, as it can be difficult to find a small set of test inputs that trigger adverse behaviors. To address this issue, we introduce a new validation method for neural networks, focusing on automatic identification of test inputs that lead to safety violations and incorporate additional novel techniques. Our goal is to set a standard for the validation of neural networks in control, similar to the one for control systems. To achieve this objective, we hold a research challenge with a public dataset to promote the sharing of methods, benchmarking, and comparison among researchers. Our results demonstrate that by combining the test of open-loop neural systems with an optimization procedure for finding harmful inputs, we can effectively improve the success rate of standard input-guided testing methods. Current approaches typically involve a meta-trained model on multiple related tasks and a set of task descriptions, allowing the model to infer task understanding from its diverse experiences. This study presents an analysis of the dynamic properties of a J1-J2 Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice, where both inter- and intra-sublattice spin exchanges are accounted for. Utilizing a Monte Carlo sampling, the dynamic structure factor is determined and compared across various parameter ranges. Notably, the research finds that the region of the phase diagram surrounding the organic triangular lattice material ETCu2(1,5-diaza-3,7-dione)2 exhibits a unique characteristic known as a spin liquid, distinct from the more conventional antiferromagnetically ordered states found in neighboring areas. To differentiate between these states, the research employs two distinct criteria: the first being the symmetry of the spin correlations, which helps distinguish ordered and liquid phases, and the second being the collinear spin correlations, which helps pinpoint the boundaries between these phases. By employing these methods, the research identifies regions that definitely host spin liquids as well as areas that may potentially host more than one phase. A kinetic model with velocity-dependent collision frequency is proposed for describing rarefied gas flows. This model builds upon the BGK model, with an extended collision frequency $\Omega(v)$ tailored to each velocity range. To derive $\Omega(v)$, a crucial simplification, known as the Chapman-Enskog expansion, is adapted for various velocity ranges. Two distinct solutions emerge, yielding two velocity-dependent collision frequencies. Consequently, a more refined model results in improved accuracy for gas flow simulations, particularly in scenarios where velocity-dependent scattering probabilities are crucial. This improvement is most noticeable when soft-intermolecular potentials are considered, further validating the model's efficacy. Moreover, model comparisons involve numerical simulations of diverse problems, with a log-scale applied to better visualize the models' discrepancies. Lastly, model-performance assessments are based on specific problem parameters and metric optimization. While the models converge for particular problem parameters and certain optimisation methods, their performance diverges, with significant discrepancies observed under different conditions and when various velocity ranges and optimization methods are considered. Consequently, a final assessment of the models' efficacy is challenging without explicit problem parameters and criteria for optimisation. Nevertheless, the models developed are both efficient and accurate, with both having potential in the study of rarefied gas dynamics. For simplicity, our discussion has primarily focused on 1-D velocity spaces although the generalisation to higher dimensions is also feasible. Moreover, the models' computational implementation is relatively straightforward with existing Fortran and C code available for the relevant BGK model simulations, with the understanding that the models' development was facilitated by the inclusion of bogus velocity ranges. Lastly, future work could productively explore alternative kinetic models for the description of rarefied gas dynamics, with a related study on this topic already being considered. Achieving this goal requires not only a thorough grasp of QCD's parton distribution functions but also a deep understanding of how partons are interconnected. To this end, data on three-nucleon gluon moments is needed, which can only be obtained through precise measurements at low to moderate momentum transfers. To produce such data, researchers must develop advanced detectors that can identify both the positioning and movement of individual particles with great accuracy, particularly at very small momentum transfers. To facilitate this process, new forward detectors are being created to fill the gap in existing detector design, while also enabling new areas of investigation, including measurements of heavy flavor jets and charm hadronization. This paper outlines the requirements for a new forward detector, discusses existing prototype development for a forward detector, and highlights the importance of a new forward detector within the broader EIC program. Additionally, we will examine the functional requirements for a forward detector system that can accurately measure low-momentum transfers while also resolving very narrow features in the momentum distribution of quarks and gluons. Given that the geometry and kinematics of the interaction region, the expected luminosity, and the characteristics of the central detector complex will influence the design of the forward detector, researchers must develop a thorough understanding of these factors to design a suitable detector that can accurately measure the desired features of the momentum distribution. Prototype development for a forward detector is currently underway, and we will outline the goals, approach, and expected outcomes of these efforts. Finally, we will acknowledge the support of an NSF-sponsored REU program that allowed undergraduate students to participate in these efforts. In 2019, scientists detected a significant outburst from the low-mass, low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (LMLAG) V599 Aql. This event was unusual because it didn't last long - the light from the event was only partially detected by the OGLE-IV survey due to interference from the moon. Now, a new paper examines this event again using new data from the OGLE-IV transit survey. These new observations confirm that the AGN on the galaxy V599 Aql experienced an outburst again in 2020, nearly two years after the initial one. This second outburst was significantly brighter than the first one and showed increased emission in the u band, while the OGLE-IV red bands detected no variability. As a result, the second outburst could be distinguished from typical photometric fluctuations caused by interference, known as "microlensing." Furthermore, the data suggest the second outburst was likely caused by a change in the AGN's accretion rate rather than a change in the physical conditions of the accretion disk. In addition, the data show that the LMLAG V599 Aql experiences continuous, minor variability - about 0.15 mag with a time scale of about 80-160 days, which may be caused by stellar microlensing. In 2021, the AGN on the galaxy V599 Aql experienced a significant outburst again, surpassing the second outburst's brightness for the first time. This event will be discussed in a separate paper. In summary, the data show that the LMLAG V599 Aql experiences unusual variability, possibly linked to the phenomenon of stellar microlensing, or the AGN's accretion rate fluctuating at the quiescent, low accretion rate state. On the other hand, the AGN's accretion rate may experience larger changes at the high accretion rate state, resulting in more intense outbursts. It's also possible that the AGN's variability behavior could be impacted by the presence of a highly inclined disk. In any case, the data show that the LMLAG V599 Aql experiences more intense outbursts than previously thought, resulting from either a change in the accretion rate or microlensing, neither of which were considered potential causes before. The spectrum of HD58260, a rapidly rotating early B-type star, exhibits narrow lines emitted in the ultraviolet spectrum, offering a direct insight into its magnetic field properties due to radiative transfer effects. Utilizing high-resolution, very sensitive spectroscopic measurements, our study determined the magnetic field geometry of HD58260 by analyzing a dataset comprising 11 observations over a 30-day period at a 0.8 m telescope. The precision of our magnetic field map was approximately 20 Gauss. The maps for HD58260 demonstrate characteristic features associated with rapid rotation, displaying stress at the equator and a rotational period of 0.32 days. Notably, the magnetic field strength decreases by approximately 80 percent from the poles to the equator. The spectral lines observed displayed center-to-lower-wing to center-to-upper-wing asymmetry, indicating Zeeman splitting, as well as increased dispersion with latitude, reaching 600 cm/s, revealing the magnetic field's influence on gas flow patterns. The magnetic field strength was found to be consistent at 800-1000 Gauss across all 11 observations. Utilizing non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE), our calculations revealed the magnetic field's impact on the formation of narrow spectral lines, as well as the magnetic field's role in gas density distributions, based on the Doppler shift. The magnetic field of HD58260 was found to be stable over short periods of time but exhibited variations in the direction of stress by as much as 36 degrees between consecutive observations. The magnetic field was determined to be responsible for the majority of observed asymmetries, as well as a magnetic field radius of approximately 0.5 times the visual radius of the star. The magnetic field of HD58260 was found not to be synchronized with its rotation period, and unlike early B-type stars with aligned magnetic field geometry in relation to inclination, our study reveals a positive correlation between magnetic field inclination and stress, suggesting the presence of a retrograde magnetic field in HD58260. The Dunkl intertwuing operator in one dimension has a representation in terms of one dimensional classical free bosons. Utilizing this representation may provide a fresh perspective on the Dunkl operator, but it could also pose challenges of moving between the operator and the corresponding coordinate representations. For instance, the free boson representation includes a zero mode that may not correspond to the traditional ground state of the Dunkl operator. Furthermore, the free boson representation lacks the symmetry inherent in the Dunkl operator, due to its non-unitary nature. Therefore, any attempt to glean insight from this representation relies on demonstrating that the non-unitary symmetry of the free boson system can still offer meaningful insights, a prospect that we examine below. Specifically, we will investigate the connection to the Bessel process. Although the standard method of connecting the Bessel process to the Dunkl operator through its action on monomials in $x^k$ is well established but laborious, the representation we propose allows for a more streamlined and concise approach. Similarly, the connection to the L\'evy process can also be reinterpreted using the free boson representation, although we note that the unitarity of the L\'evy process means that the non-unitary symmetry of the free boson system will not provide any new insights in this instance. In any case, we will begin by providing a representation-theoretic description of the Dunkl intertwining operator using the one-dimensional classical free boson system, before proceeding to examine the connections to the Bessel process and the L\'evy process. Ultimately, we will conclude with some general considerations about the representation of the Dunkl operator in one dimension. The primary benefit of using the free boson representation in this way is the insight it offers into the action of the Dunkl operator on non-monomial states, although we acknowledge that the non-unitary symmetry of the free boson system will not provide any new insights in instances where the unitarity of the underlying stochastic process can be relied upon. In any case, we hope that the methodological approach we use to connect the free boson system to the Bessel process and the L\'evy process via the Dunkl operator may provide some fresh perspectives on this system, even if the non-unitary symmetry of the free boson system means that the results will primarily be of theoretical interest. This article examines the convergence characteristics of a novel, nonparametric estimator for the conditional expectation function in multiple dimensions.  It introduces a versatile family of estimators that can be tailored to prioritize either interval-specific or kernel estimates of the conditional expectation, and explores their performance in various scenarios.  It is shown that with an appropriately selected smoothing parameter, the proposed estimator achieves optimal minimax risk rates, and that there are no nonparametric estimators that can achieve a lower rate of error when the underlying distribution is uniform on a compact interval.  Furthermore, a method for selecting the smoothing parameter is developed and is shown to be more effective than traditional techniques in high-dimensional spaces.  The findings are corroborated with simulation studies and illustrated by an analysis of a challenging dataset from point process theory.  A comparison with the traditional kernel-smoothing method reveals that the novel estimator can often perform better or equally well on this particular task. Online Federated Learning (OFL) has gained momentum as a means to deploy machine learning models on a wide-scale, due to its capability to process data in an online setting. Given various participants and devices, it is necessary for the model updates to be asynchronous in nature. Nonetheless, the absence of synchronization results in uneven data sharing, impacting the convergence speed and efficiency. To overcome this challenge, we present an innovative asynchronous FL approach, where the central server ensures consistent and efficient convergence by the proper timing of data sharing and model updates. Building upon this concept, we develop an asynchronous online FL framework for nonlinear regression tasks. The framework differentiates itself by addressing the nonlinear relationship between features and target variables, as well as considering the nonlinear regression problem in the presence of errors. The proposed framework includes two iterations - the first involves parameter update in an asynchronous manner through federated averaging, while the second ensures synchronization of model updates and imposes a l1 penalty on the regression coefficients to eliminate redundant features. Experimental findings using real-world datasets, including energy consumption data and medical cost data, demonstrate that the proposed framework leads to a considerable reduction in communication steps and convergence time while maintaining a comparable accuracy level. To support this discovery, we present a computational analysis that verifies the conditions for convergence and stability of the proposed asynchronous FL approach. Furthermore, we show through the energy consumption dataset, the proposed framework can save 78.2% of energy, 65.7% of time, and 6.1% of the width of the participating devices while maintaining a comparable regression accuracy. Wildfires pose a significant threat to global communities, and their destructive impact is amplified by rapid observation methods using visible and infrared imaging. Recent image fusion techniques have improved monitoring and detection, but most existing approaches fall short due to several limitations. Traditional methods, such as pixel-by-pixel multiplication, are unsuitable for practical use, while deep learning-based techniques exhibit better performance but are often fixed and cannot adapt to new datasets. Furthermore, existing methodologies rely on pre-defined guidelines, which may not accurately capture the characteristics of wildfires. To address these limitations, our research proposes a new framework, FIRe-GAN. By leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks, FIRe-GAN learns the optimal weight for combining visible and infrared images, enabling more effective multi-spectral wildfire observation. Our results demonstrate that FIRe-GAN surpasses existing fusion methods in both objective evaluation and visual assessments. Given the unpredictability of wildfires, FIRe-GAN is also capable of adapting to new datasets with different conditions, making it a more practical choice for real-world applications. However, determining optimal premium rates can be complicated by the interdependence of claim sizes, which poses an unsolved problem. Recent research by Zheng and Chen (2022) introduced a novel deep learning approach for estimating insurance premium formulas. Their method employs a neural network to find a solution for the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, an optimal control problem related to insurance coverage. Building upon this foundation, this paper extends the scope of problems by incorporating additional constraints. A case study involving real-life data illustrates the applicability of our approach in analyzing loss runs for insurance policies. However, our method cannot guarantee convergence due to the presence of these constraints. In practice, we recommend periodic re-evaluation of the network using updated data sets to ensure the highest level of service. Nevertheless, the absence of theoretical convergence proof may impede the adoption of our approach by solvency regulators, an issue that requires further exploration by the academic community. The proliferation of geotagged social media data on the web offers considerable possibilities for building location-based applications and inferring implicit user data. Implicitly agreeing to share geotagged data with service providers, users grant those providers permission to use their data, yet questions persist about the explicit details of those services. This research aims to demonstrate that using social media geotags can provide explicit information, such as determining whether a user is a local or tourist by analyzing their activity patterns over time. To this end, we developed VALUE, a large scale platform that uses collective human judgment to infer implicit user data from geotags. By leveraging micro-votes from users over feature-specific questions, we can provide individualized answers for each user. As an example, we can determine an individual's local scale (residential area, city, state, or country) by their voting history. The VALUE platform consists of three key components: (1) feature extraction, (2) data cleaning, and (3) inference. The first component extracts fundamental features (such as time, place, and content), which are later cleaned and validated with control questions to filter out noise and detect valuers. Finally, we provide answers for individual users based on their features and the voting history of the crowd. Using Facebook's Open Graph data, we evaluated VALUE on its accuracy in local scale inference and discovered notable patterns, such as urban users providing implicit collaboration among each other to infer accurate answers for explicit local inference. Furthermore, we provided explicit answers for implicit local inference based on users' activity patterns. The results of our research revealed that using social media geotags can provide explicit information, such as determining whether a user is a local or tourist by analyzing their activity patterns over time. The VALUE platform achieves an accuracy of 86.7% for determining the user's local scale or country and 83.7% for the city or state based on individual-specific features and voting history. The research also provides implicit details of geotag-based services for explicit local inference. The value of the VALUE platform lies in its accurate inference of local-scale answers based on users' voting history over time, which can provide collective human judgment for various location-based applications and infer implicit user data from geotags. The research reveals the explicit details of geotag-based services for local-scale inference and provides the social media geotags with explicit information, which can alleviate the persistence of explicit questions about the implicit user data from geotag providers. In seismic reflectivity inversion, the non-uniform sparse framework has been widely used to address problems such as wavelet-type ambiguity and proxy-based forward modeling. A key challenge lies in the sparsity promotion term's non-smooth and non-differentiable nature. To address these issues, we present a novel deep learning method based on a proximal average network to solve non-smooth optimization problems, where the problem can be reformulated as the sum of a differentiable term and a non-smooth term. This method leverages the proximal mapping and subgradient of the non-smooth term to create a network trainable via backpropagation. We have also developed a training scheme for the network, implemented in PyTorch. We test the network's performance in a multi-scale seismic inversion context, reformulating the sparsity promotion term as the sum of Laplacian-based and Hadamard-based terms. Compared to the Laplacian-based term, the Hadamard-based term has a coarser sparsity pattern, reducing the network's redundancy. We evaluate our network's performance using synthetic data from a Sigsbee-2A benchmark 2D seismic survey. The results indicate that the network can be trained to approximate the proximal average mapping, maintaining its effectiveness even when the network parameter p is changed. We also demonstrate that the network generalizes well to the actual seismic data, achieving a high data acquisition efficiency of 94%. The network presents sparse inversion results comparable to those of the conventional MESP method, while its differentiable property enables an automatic and efficient seismic data acquisition scheme via conventional gradient-based optimization algorithms. We also conduct a further evaluation via a 3D seismic reflection experiment from the Valhall field. The results show that the network can be trained to approximate the proximal average mapping not only within the non-smooth term but also in the entire cost function. This property allows for a reduction in the number of network layers. The network's performance in the 3D case is similar to that in the 2D case, with a network data acquisition efficiency of 93.6%. The network presents a data-driven approach to non-uniform sparse framework solvers, showing potential in seismic inversion and other non-smooth optimization problems. The network's performance in the 2D and 3D cases suggests a promising future in other optimization problems. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA spaces, specifically BMOA and its subspaces BMOA_s and BMOA_p. BMOA represents the Bergman-like space of analytic functions on the unit disk, while BMOA_s and BMOA_p correspond to Hardy-like spaces for the given classes of functions. We focus on three main parameters: the composition, Volterra type, and expansion semigroups. We establish criteria and, in certain instances, directly calculate sufficient and necessary conditions for these semigroups to exist for given function families. We further examine operator norms within these semigroups. Additionally, this article compares the obtained results with those from analogous studies on BMOA-like spaces for the bi-disc and polydisc cases. Crucially, it is demonstrated that certain maximal subsystems of BMOA_p fail to form semigroups under composition, a distinction not observed in BMOA. This work also highlights a surprising equivalence between the Volterra type semigroup's existence in BMOA_p and a specific, previously established conjecture. We resolve this conjecture, previously proposed by Zhao et al. (2018) for BMOA. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task in language research used to supply context for sentence completion systems, automatic text summarization, and other applications. For historical documents, no single system has consistently achieved reliable results. This study presents a novel approach to develop a dependable system for annotating POS in historical texts: set-valued POS tagging. This adaptable method can reduce errors resulting from linguistic model inaccuracy and overcome the limited accuracy of automated historical tagging, which is currently around 40\%. When a set-valued tag is assigned to a word, it accounts for potential ambiguities arising from linguistic models or data limitations. The proposed system demonstrates a significant error reduction of up to 50\% on standardized datasets. Moreover, the systematic evaluation of the suggested architecture provides valuable insights for builders on set-valued tagging and out-of-vocabulary words, ultimately resulting in more reliable historical text annotation. This research provides a computational solution to historical text annotation that can be adapted and expanded to address other linguistic tasks and datasets. In the general context of regular categories, a categorical characterization of preorders and equivalence relations can be established based on the existence of certain biproducts. Specifically, it is shown that a relation is an equivalence relation within a preorder if and only if it yields a cocartesian representation in the preorder. Furthermore, it is proven that every preoder has a unique largest equivalence relation, which serves as a cocartesian extension, and that two relations produce the same equivalence relation if and only if they coincide on their associated cocartesian extensions. These findings encompass and significantly generalize previously established results in the context of directed sets. Moreover, it is acknowledged that in certain categories, despite the availability of a comprehensive characterization of equivalence relations as coproductive closures of monomorphisms, a universal characterization of preorders does not exist. Ultimately, it is recognized that in the context of complete atomic categories possessing choice properties, a characterization of preorders analogous to that in $\mathbf{Set}$ can be established. Specifically, it is demonstrated that a preoder is a complete atomic preorder if and only if every binary relation that is symmetric and connected is an equivalence relation within the relation. Consequently, a universal characterization of equivalence relations can be established within the realm of complete atomic posets possessing choice properties. Various additional results concerning the fundamental properties of relations in the context of regular categories are also provided. Moreover, it is noted that while some of these findings can be seen as natural generalizations of established results in the context of $\mathbf{Set}$, they may not be readily deducible from existing literature on the subject, which is primarily based on the work of Manes. Finally, it is acknowledged that in certain categories, relations that are symmetric and connected do not necessarily form a complete atomic preorder, as evidenced by the symmetric powerset relation in the category of finitely presented monoids. A brief description of potential research directions inspired by these findings is also provided. The paper ultimately concludes by establishing a characterization of preorders and equivalence relations within the context of well-founded categories possessing biproducts. The evidence suggests that in the absence of choice properties, a characterization of equivalence relations as coproductive closures of monomorphisms may not be feasible, whereas a characterization of preorders may be possible, potentially paving the way for a characterization of well-founded sets with biproducts. Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn general image-text associations without the need for specialized annotations. However, its performance is still limited compared to other state-of-the-art models that also rely on Visual-Language Pre-training. This research demonstrates that a significant factor contributing to these limitations is the absence of directedness in pre-training text data. To address this challenge, we introduce Visual-directed CLIP (VT-CLIP), a method that enhances visual-directed text pre-training to complement Visual-Language Pre-training models. We establish three critical elements for VT-CLIP: (1) we introduce the visual directionality criterion to evaluate the alignment of image and text features, with the text features prompted by specific images; (2) we establish a new dataset, iFlickr-Concept365, which integrates visual directionality, by linking concept labels with the top ones derived from image embeddings for each idea, thereby forming triplet pairs: concept, concept idea, and an image representing the top idea; (3) we apply a two-stage refinement of CLIP models, initially using the existing CLIP models to get initial image-text embeddings and then pre-training the model with the refined embeddings on the iFlickr-Concept365 dataset, to improve the model's visual-directed capacity. Through extensive evaluations on typical CLIP tasks, we observe VT-CLIP achieves a notable 2% or higher absolute improvements over strong Visual-Language Pre-training models, to be precise, our method achieves an 8% or higher improvement over all tested datasets. The proposed VT-CLIP is also shown to surpass state-of-art models on semantic segmentation, anisotropic distribution and image captioning tasks. The proposed approach is versatile and can be adapted for other models, not restricted to CLIP models. The proposed knowledge can be further used to design programs that can collaborate with humans more effectively, particularly in scenarios where visual-direction is a critical factor. By decomposing the noisy system into equivalent state-space equations and establishing a connection between the operator AARE's solution and the solutions to two corresponding quadratic matrix inequalities, our methodology accommodates various forms of disturbance, including multiplicative and additive cases. By leveraging existing numerical methods to find the necessary system matrices, our approach yields a solution to the operator AARE, which can be used to define a non-discriminating operator and address an optimal control problem. Ultimately, this research expands the capabilities of numerical methods to solve small- to medium-scale problems. Furthermore, numerical examples are utilized to demonstrate the applicability of our findings to solving operator AAREs in systems disturbed by multiplicative or additive factors. The application of artificial intelligence in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is undergoing rapid transformation.  Despite growing interest in standardizing this field, there is currently a lack of tools promoting interoperability, leading to numerous working groups and toolsets developing new standards without a clear understanding of existing resources, ultimately causing market saturation and a lack of user adoption.  To address this, we introduce highdicom, an open-source, community-driven Python library for data exchange formats commonly used in pathology and radiology image analysis.  Highdicom provides tools for working with digital images, model outputs, and quality control metrics in standardized formats, as well as supporting widely used standards such as DICOM and ANONYMIZE.  By making highdicom's source code and documentation publicly accessible, we aim to promote user adoption and standardization in this rapidly evolving field.  To date, the highdicom library has already received support from over 200 individuals from over 100 organizations worldwide, further highlighting the need for a clear and standardized data exchange framework.  By promoting standardization and providing a stable, open-source toolset, highdicom is poised to help the medical imaging community effectively share and disseminate model outputs and annotation data.  As such, we invite users to adopt highdicom and engage with the growing community to shape and evolve the future of data exchange formats within the medical imaging field.  Additionally, we include a detailed guide on getting started with highdicom, as well as a set of comprehensive API documentation and example use cases to facilitate user adoption and community engagement.  We hope to establish a collaborative community within the highdicom GitHub repository, the IMI Standardization for Artificial Intelligence in Imaging (https://imi-ehealth.eu/std-ai-imaging), and the open-source toolset itself to promote standardization and provide a stable, community-driven data exchange framework moving forward.  Ultimately, the development and evolution of highdicom is intended to serve the broader medical imaging community, serving as a model for other fields to standardize their own data exchange formats and processes.  As such, we welcome and invite various stakeholders to join the highdicom community and collaborate on establishing a clear and standardized data exchange framework moving forward.
